Zirconia is a common coating material used for thermal barrier coatings.
Radiation becomes more significant as temperatures are raised for higher efficiency in advanced engines.
The two-flux method is used to model the radiative contribution within the semitransparent thermal barrier coating.
The paper considers two cases for the external surface of the thermal barrier coating: 1) with an opaque soot layer, and 2) with a clean exposed surface.
If the zirconia becomes covered with soot, the metal temperatures are increased due to the soot absorbing the incident radiation.
For a clean thermal barrier coating, the semitransparency of the zirconia can decrease temperatures in the zirconia compared to an opaque coating.
The radiative effects are relatively too small to provide sufficient benefit from scattering for turbine blades with high convective heat transfer coefficients.
Semitransparency is found to be beneficial for limited conditions, as it can increase the effective coating thermal conductivity for heating primarily by convection.
The semitransparent region of a zirconia thermal barrier coating extends to a cutoff wavelength of about 5 μm.
The paper provides an analytical procedure using the two-flux method to account for radiative heat transfer within the thermal barrier coating.
Illustrative solutions are presented for typical conditions in an aircraft engine.
The absorption optical thickness of zirconia thermal barrier coatings is small, and the scattering albedo is close to one.
The shooting method used for solving the two-point boundary value problem for the radiative flux converged without difficulty for the given conditions.
The iteration method changes when the zirconia coating has an opaque soot layer on its exposed surface.
For a 1-mm-thick zirconia coating, the metal temperature is substantially reduced compared to the uncoated metal.
